examples.problem_statement: A cat travels at a speed of 60 inches/second. How long will it take this cat, in seconds, to travel 300 feet? (12 inches = 1 foot)

solution.description: The question asks about a distance in feet, so first convert the given rate out of inches per second by multiplying it by the conversion factor 1 foot per 12 inches.
Everything is now expressed in feet and seconds, so substitute the converted rate and the given distance into the rate-time-distance formula.
Solve the equation from the previous step for the unknown time by dividing the distance by the rate.

key_reminders: Convert every quantity into a single consistent unit system before applying a rate formula.
The rate-time-distance relationship is r \times t = d.
12 inches = 1 foot, so dividing an inches-per-second rate by 12 gives feet per second.
common_mistakes: Converting the distance 300 feet into inches but leaving the rate in inches per second and then reporting the answer in the wrong unit.
Multiplying by 12 instead of dividing by 12 when turning 60 inches per second into feet per second.

concept.technique_name: Pythagorean theorem then area-matching to find a missing side

examples.problem_statement: Triangle ABC and Rectangle JKLM have equal areas. In Triangle ABC the leg BC measures 12 and the hypotenuse AC measures 15, with the right angle at B; Rectangle JKLM has one side measuring 6. What is the perimeter of Rectangle JKLM?

solution.description: Apply the Pythagorean theorem to the right triangle, squaring the known leg 12 and the known hypotenuse 15 to set up an equation in the unknown side AB.
Isolate (AB)^2 and take the square root to get the missing leg; this is a 9-12-15 triangle, a 3-4-5 triangle with every measurement tripled.
Now that both legs are known, use the triangle area formula with 12 as the base and 9 as the height.
The rectangle has the same area, 54, and one side is 6, so divide to solve for the other side of the rectangle.
With both rectangle side lengths known, apply the rectangle perimeter formula, doubling the sum of the two sides.

key_reminders: In a right triangle, leg^2 + leg^2 = hypotenuse^2.
The area of a triangle is \frac{1}{2} \times \text{base} \times \text{height}; for a right triangle the two legs serve as base and height.
Equal areas let you transfer a computed area from one figure to another and solve for a missing dimension.
common_mistakes: Treating 12 and 15 as the two legs and computing a hypotenuse instead of recognizing 15 as the hypotenuse, which gives a wrong AB.
Stopping at JM = 9 and reporting the side length rather than the requested perimeter.
Reporting 6 + 9 = 15 as the perimeter by forgetting to double the sum of the sides.

concept.technique_name: picking numbers to test a quantitative comparison, including the value zero

examples.problem_statement:
x is a non-negative even integer.
Quantity A: x
Quantity B: 1
(A) Quantity A is greater. (B) Quantity B is greater. (C) The two quantities are equal. (D) The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.

solution.result: 0 is an allowed value of x
solution.description: Read the phrasing carefully: the problem says non-negative rather than positive, which is the test-writer's sneaky signal that 0 is permitted alongside the positive even integers.

solution.result: Quantity B is greater; eliminate (A) and (C)
solution.description: Test the boundary value 0 first, since ZONEF reminds you to try 0 whenever it is allowed, and compare the two quantities for that value.
Test a positive even integer such as 2, which reverses the comparison and rules out the remaining single-relationship choice.
Because different permitted values of x produce different relationships, no single comparison holds, so the relationship cannot be determined.

key_reminders: Non-negative means positive values and 0; only positive excludes 0.
In quantitative comparison, if two allowed values of the variable give opposite comparisons, the answer is (D).
ZONEF prompts you to test Zero, One, Negatives, Extremes, and Fractions when the constraints allow them.
common_mistakes: Reading non-negative as positive, testing only x = 2, 4, 6, and choosing (A).
Stopping after the x = 0 case and choosing (B) without testing a positive even value.
